entry.title: Literature Review: Matryoshka LM Suites
entry.content:
Related Work & Literature Foundations

Matryoshka LM Suites builds at the intersection of two major paradigms in efficient language modeling: cross-model knowledge transfer (distillation and speculative decoding) and parameter-nested model consolidation (elastic sub-networks and representation learning).

1. Cross-Model Knowledge Transfer

Speculative Decoding & Draft Generation

Speculative decoding relies on the asymmetry between memory-bandwidth-bound token generation and compute-bound parallel verification. Leviathan et al. (2023) demonstrated that a lightweight draft model can propose candidate token sequences validated in parallel by a larger target model without altering the output distribution.

While classic speculative decoding requires maintaining and synchronizing two independently trained models, Matryoshka LM Suites enables the target (verifier) and nested draft (proposer) models to be trained within a single execution graph. This addresses latency and deployment overhead by ensuring architectural alignment between draft and verifier from pre-training onward.

Knowledge Distillation: Sequential to Concurrent

Foundational distillation (Hinton et al., 2015; Gou et al., 2021 survey) established the standard two-stage pipeline: pre-training a high-capacity teacher and subsequently transferring its soft probabilities or hidden states to a compact student.

Recent work has focused on closing the efficiency gap between teacher and student via online distillation (Peng et al., 2024) and mutual learning (Zhang et al., 2018). Matryoshka LM Suites pushes this to its logical conclusion: the “student” is an embedded architectural subset of the “teacher,” allowing bidirectional gradient signals and removing the need for a separate offline distillation phase.

2. Parameter Nesting & Elastic Model Architectures

Matryoshka Representations to Elastic Networks

A work which shares the Matryoshka nickname and provided inspiration for the authors is Matryoshka Representation Learning (MRL) (Kusupati et al., 2022), by training vectors whose leading dimensions function as accurate, low-dimensional embeddings in their own right. By structuring representations like Russian nesting dolls—where early dimensions capture core semantic signals and trailing dimensions encode fine-grained nuance—a single embedding can serve multiple resource budgets MatFormer (Devvrit et al., 2023) extended this principle from static vectors to transformer weights, training nested sub-networks across feed-forward and attention blocks. While MatFormer demonstrated that multiple model granularities can coexist inside a single set of weights, it introduced structural complexities for memory reuse—notably non-contiguous KV-cache layouts during variable-capacity decoding.

KV-Cache Preservation & Joint-Training Efficiency

Matryoshka LM Suites directly addresses the deployment bottlenecks of previous elastic transformers:

  • KV-Cache Alignment: Ensures that nested models share consistent head dimensions and grouped-query configurations, avoiding cache fragmentation across draft and full models.
  • Compute Amortization: Rather than paying the prohibitive cost of training an entire model family (e.g., 1B, 3B, and 8B variants) independently, joint nested training extracts multiple Pareto-optimal deployment targets from a single pre-training budget.
Dimension Standard Pipeline MatFormer (2023) Matryoshka LM Suites
Model Coupling Independent weights Nested sub-matrices Nested sub-architectures
Distillation / Speculation Post-hoc / Multi-stage Independent downstream Natively co-trained draft/verifier
KV-Cache Reuse Incompatible across models Requires restructuring Shared cache-compatible geometry
entry.summary: Contextualizing Matryoshka LM Suites within speculative decoding, knowledge distillation, and nested/elastic transformer architectures.

entry.title: The minds behind Matryoshka
entry.content:
Nathan Godey

Nathan Godey is a researcher in natural language processing and machine learning whose work focuses on language modeling, model representations, and training efficiency. His research explores how language models learn and how their architectures and training methods can be improved.

Matryoshka Language Model Suites fits closely into this research profile. The paper investigates how models of different sizes can be trained within a shared architecture, reducing training costs while maintaining performance. This extends his broader interest in developing more efficient and effective language models.

Yoav Artzi

Yoav Artzi is a computer scientist and researcher in natural language processing and machine learning. His research has covered language understanding and generation, interactive language systems, and methods for training models to perform complex language tasks.

Matryoshka Language Model Suites fits into his broader research through its focus on improving language model training and deployment. Although the paper is more concerned with model architecture and computational efficiency than with interactive systems or language understanding, it aligns with his wider interest in advancing language modeling methods and making them more effective in practice.
entry.summary: The paper closely aligns with Nathan Godey’s research on efficient language model design and complements Yoav Artzi’s broader work on advancing language modeling methods.

entry.title: The Authors’ Path of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

link.title: The Authors’ Path of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

entry.content:
Get to Know the Authors

Nathan Godey

Nathan Godey is a Post-doctoral Associate working in Yoav Artzi’s lab at Cornell University. Godey’s research is mostly driven by understanding and improving the representations of language models.

Yoav Artzi

Yoav Artzi is a Professor at Cornell University and a Visiting Researcher at Google DeepMind. His lab, Cornell Language, Interaction, and Learning (LIL), primarily focuses on natural language modeling, processing, and learning.

Matryoshka LM and the Rest of Their Research

Godey’s PhD thesis revolves around improving language models, whether by optimizing training time, generation time, memory usage, or perplexity. These principles are reflected on all of Godey’s work, especially on his recent work with Artzi. The two develop new architectures, as well as pinpointing architectural bottlenecks such as the LM head.

Some New Architectures

  • The Matryoshka LM suite cuts training time (among other optimizations) for a family of similar models of different sizes.
  • Copy-Paste LMs introduce new types of tokens and and create a pointer mechanism to yield better models (improved performance across training time, generation time, memory usage, and perplexity).
  • Continuous-query limited memory language models (CO-LMLM) achieve lower perplexity than models trained on significantly more data. Instead of relying solely on the model’s parameters, the mechanism retrieves data from an external unstructured knowledge base triggered by a special token.
  • Implement Memory sharing in Loop Transformers (LT) to reduce perplexity.

entry.title: <Critique / literature review / follow-ups> of
entry.content:
Follow-ups worth doing

The question. In Section 3.2.3, the Matryoshka pair fits a batch of 102 sequences in 80GB, versus 64 for the Vanilla pair. Throughput rises with batch size on its own. Were the Figure 5 throughput numbers measured at each pair’s own maximum batch size, and how much of the reported gain (up to 26% over the Vanilla pair) comes from better draft-verifier agreement rather than the larger batch?

The experiment. Compare the Vanilla and Matryoshka pairs at the same batch size (at most 64 on an 80GB GPU, where the Vanilla pair maxes out), then run the Matryoshka pair at its own maximum of 102, using the same setup as Figure 5. The gap at equal batch size reflects draft-verifier agreement; the extra gap at 102 reflects the larger batch. Why it’s worth doing. The paper credits the speedup mainly to higher acceptance from shared weights and distillation, but reports accepted length only about 5% higher on average under nucleus sampling, while throughput is up 14% at the headline setting. These are not identical measurements, so this is only a hint. A matched-batch result would show whether the alignment benefit stands on its own, or whether much of the gain is the memory saving, which is a real benefit but a different one.

Status. Question sent to the authors (Nathan Godey, Yoav Artzi) on . No reply yet.

entry.title: Copyediting Section 1 (Introduction) of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

link.title: Copyediting Section 1 (Introduction) of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

entry.content:
What I changed and why

The original introduction repeats its three main points (stacking, distillation, speculative decoding) three times: in the middle paragraphs, in a summary paragraph, and finally in the bullet points. For example: “…the nested structure further benefits speculative decoding”, and then: “Moreover, the shared-weight structure and low-cost distillation substantially improves cross-model agreement and makes larger draft models practical for speculative decoding.” and then: “We demonstrate that the shared-weight structure and low-cost distillation substantially improve cross-model agreement and make larger drafts practical for speculative decoding…“

This makes it longer than it needs to be. I removed the repetition by deleting the redundant sentences in the summary paragraph—keeping only the unique details like the dataset and code release—and leaving the original bullet points intact. I also simplified the opening sentence so it gets straight to the engineering problem without using passive language.

Before and after

Before

The way training and inference costs of large language models (LLMs) scale steeply with model size creates a demand for models across a broad spectrum of sizes, from 100M [Allal et al., 2025] to trillion [DeepSeek-AI, 2026] parameters, for diverse deployment scenarios. Delivering models from different scales allows for different load/performance tradeoffs, with smaller models being more memory- and compute-efficient than their larger counterparts. As a result, models are usually released in suites: groups of models trained separately on similar data, with smaller models often distilled from larger ones in the suite. The question of efficiency in training and serving model suites jointly is rarely studied. We propose a training framework that is particularly well-suited to the model-suite paradigm and offers several concrete benefits over the standard approach.

Instead of training separate models, our approach progressively stacks the outputs of smaller sub-models as inputs to larger ones. For instance, rather than training a {1B, 8B, 30B, 70B} suite as four independent runs, our method trains a single architecture combining a 1B sub-model with additional 7B, 22B, and 40B parameter blocks, resulting in 70B trained parameters instead of 109B. Contrarily to previous work [Devvrit et al., 2023], each sub-model can be detached as a standalone language model, with its own depth and KV cache footprint, and served independently just like a regular checkpoint. This setup also makes distillation from the largest model to all smaller ones a natural by-product, as logits from all submodels are available during training. As a result, training the Matryoshka suite costs on the same order as training only the largest model alone, and delivers all N sub-models in a single run, with cheap knowledge distillation.

At inference time, the nested structure further benefits speculative decoding [Leviathan et al., 2023]: the draft model is nested in the verifier model, and both already share KV cache, eliminating the usual memory overhead of maintaining a separate draft model. Cross-model prediction agreement is also higher than in independently trained suites, directly increasing token acceptance rates.

We verify our approach by training a 3B-parameter Matryoshka suite with 500M, 1.5B, and 3B sub-models on 35B tokens from the FineWeb-Edu dataset. Our suite matches independently trained baselines on validation perplexity, out-of-domain perplexity, and benchmark performance while using 36% less total training compute. Moreover, the shared-weight structure and low-cost distillation substantially improves cross-model agreement and makes larger draft models practical for speculative decoding. We also conduct an extensive analysis of architectural design, and show the impact of width and depth configurations in Matryoshka suites, and that both the distillation loss and our model junction mechanism are crucial for the performance of smaller sub-models. We release trained checkpoints and a HuggingFace’s transformers-compatible implementation.

Overall, our contributions can be summarized as:

  • We introduce Matryoshka Language Model Suites, a pretraining framework that nests sub-models of increasing width and depth into a single jointly trained architecture (Section 2);
  • We derive a low-cost distillation objective that leverages the availability of all sub-model logits at every forward pass;
  • We train a 3B-parameter Matryoshka suite and show it reaches near-parity (within 0.5 average points at every size) with independently trained baselines on standard benchmarks while using 36% less training compute (Section 3);
  • We demonstrate that the shared-weight structure and low-cost distillation substantially improve cross-model agreement and make larger drafts practical for speculative decoding, where plain vanilla speculative decoding barely improves over autoregressive inference.
  • We provide extensive ablations at smaller scale (50M/100M/200M suite) that provide insights for architectural hyperparameters and training objectives.

After

The steep training and inference costs of large language models (LLMs) create a demand for models across a broad spectrum of sizes, from 100M [Allal et al., 2025] to trillion [DeepSeek-AI, 2026] parameters. As a result, models are usually released in suites: groups of models trained separately on similar data, with smaller models often distilled from larger ones. The question of efficiency in training and serving model suites jointly is rarely studied. We propose a training framework that offers several concrete benefits over the standard approach.

Instead of training separate models, our approach progressively stacks the outputs of smaller sub-models as inputs to larger ones. For instance, rather than training a {1B, 8B, 30B, 70B} suite as four independent runs, our method trains a single architecture resulting in 70B trained parameters instead of 109B. Contrarily to previous work [Devvrit et al., 2023], each sub-model can be detached as a standalone language model, with its own depth and KV cache footprint, and served independently. This setup also makes distillation from the largest model to all smaller ones a natural by-product, as logits from all submodels are available during training.

At inference time, the nested structure further benefits speculative decoding [Leviathan et al., 2023]: the draft model is nested in the verifier model, and both already share KV cache, eliminating the usual memory overhead of maintaining a separate draft model. Cross-model prediction agreement is also higher than in independently trained suites, directly increasing token acceptance rates.

Overall, our contributions can be summarized as:

  • We introduce Matryoshka Language Model Suites, a pretraining framework that nests sub-models of increasing width and depth into a single jointly trained architecture (Section 2);
  • We derive a low-cost distillation objective that leverages the availability of all sub-model logits at every forward pass;
  • We train a 3B-parameter Matryoshka suite on 35B tokens from the FineWeb-Edu dataset and show it reaches near-parity (within 0.5 average points at every size) with independently trained baselines on standard benchmarks while using 36% less training compute (Section 3);
  • We demonstrate that the shared-weight structure and low-cost distillation substantially improve cross-model agreement and make larger drafts practical for speculative decoding, where plain vanilla speculative decoding barely improves over autoregressive inference.
  • We provide extensive ablations at smaller scale (50M/100M/200M suite) that provide insights for architectural hyperparameters and training objectives.
  • We release trained checkpoints and a HuggingFace’s transformers-compatible implementation.

The general rule

Don’t repeat your summary. If you explain your main points in the text, you don’t need to summarize them again right before the bullet points. Remove sentences that state the obvious or repeat facts already mentioned, and move experimental details straight into the contribution list.

entry.title: Figure 2 in layers and dimentions annotations in the Matryoshka article

link.title: Figure 2 in layers and dimentions annotations in the Matryoshka article

entry.content:
The original

Figure 2 of Godey and Artzi’s Matryoshka Language Model Suites shows different options for number_of_layers in a 500M / 1.5B / 3B nested Matriyushka model configuration. The 2 triangles each show a different value of each of the possible configurations. One is for per-token FLOPs and the second compares the KV cache.
In order to read the graph, from each point take parallel lines to do 3 sides of the triangle, take their intersection point with each of the sides and this is the chosen configuration. Each specific configuration will so have different values at each of the 2 triangles. The markings/ticks on the sides show what percentage of the layers are of each of the nested models. The chosen configuration was of the gold-star marking, it was (24, 10, 5). The empty areas are the non possible options as outlined in Appendix D

Therefore, in order to understand a specific configuration, one must take the percentage chosen, multiply it by 39 (as this is the total number of layers chosen by the authors as a constraint) and this is the number of layers. For example, the golden star configuration has its layers of 24 + 10 + 5 = 39 as all possible configuration must be!

The redesign

A scalable version is also available: open the SVG.

The ticks have now changed, they show not only the actualy number layers instead of a percentage that isn’t divisble by 39 easily, but they also show the possible embedding dimension throughout the model! Side L_0 still shows the 500M model, L_1 the 1.5B one and L_2 the 3B one. Near each of the number_of_layers there is a D_i number that shows the possible embedding layer dimension.

What changed and why

  • Integer ticks replace fractions. Reading the fractions and might be a bit unintutive to explain the results
  • Every tick has a embedding layer dimension label. The important change was the addition of the hidden embedding dimension at each nested model. The range of possible values is given by the article’s formula of Pᵢ = 2V(Dᵢ − Dᵢ₋₁) + 16LᵢDᵢ², then selecting the possible number of attention heads. The ranges can vary due to dimensions of the previous nested models (in L_1 and L_2). So, each tick shows the range! Notice that these ranges are infered mathematically and not ones that are published.

The important change is the second one and the reason is to understand why some confiugrations are not possible. The white area with no values at the 2 triangles has no explanation at the figure itself and the appendix does give the explanation but requires the reader to do manual calculations in order to check and see it for themselves. Therefore, adding the possible dimensions sizes and seeing how they decrease as the number of layers goes up (and vise versa) makes the calculation much easier, allowing the user understand how the equation of D_0<D_1<D_2 comes into play visually and intuitively. (Since no model can be narrower that its predocessor)
entry.summary: changing the paper's triangles' ticks with layer counts and possible embedding dimensions for easier undderstanding

entry.title: Is nesting the cheapest way to build a model suite?

link.title: Is nesting the cheapest way to build a model suite?

entry.content:
The paper (Godey & Artzi, 2026) is mostly about saving compute. One nested training run gives you a 500M, a 1.5B and a 3B model for 36% less compute than training them separately, and speculative decoding gets 14–26% faster, with quality about the same. But all of those numbers come from one setup: a single training budget, draft–verifier pair, baseline and distillation loss, with all blocks always trained together. Each follow-up below changes one of these, to check whether nesting really is the cheapest way to build and run the nested models (the “dolls”). I call each nested model an exit: the point in the network where you stop and read off that model’s prediction through its own output layer. Vanilla means a model of the same size trained on its own. The follow-ups go roughly from cheapest to most expensive.

1. Does parity hold past 35B tokens?

Why this part: the 36% only matters if quality holds where small models are actually trained, and the paper stops at 35B tokens.

Question. The paper’s curves (Figures 3 and 4) track the gap to vanilla up to 35B tokens, about 11 tokens per parameter for the 3B. That is even below the roughly 20 tokens per parameter that Chinchilla found gives the best model for a fixed training budget. Small models that actually ship are trained far longer: a model that answers millions of queries costs more to run than to train, so it pays to over-train a small model rather than serve a bigger one. SmolLM2’s 1.7B, for example, saw about 11T tokens, roughly 6,500 per parameter (Allal et al., 2025). Does the gap to vanilla grow with more training (one 500M block has to serve three models) or shrink (the small exits keep learning from the 3B, at no extra cost in a nested run)?

Experiment. The authors’ Hugging Face page has checkpoints up to 60B tokens with vanilla counterparts, plus an unpublished four-exit 100M / 300M / 600M / 1B suite trained to 105B. Compare every exit with its vanilla counterpart at every checkpoint. The cleanest pairs are the 500M exit (up to 60B tokens) and the four-exit suite’s 100M (up to 105B, about 900 tokens per parameter), because their vanilla twins have exactly the same shape. One catch: a model only reaches its final quality after the learning rate is lowered at the end of training (the “cooldown”), and mid-run checkpoints haven’t had that yet. So give both models a short cooldown at two or three points, as the paper did for its compute-matched vanilla baseline (cooled down from 21B to 23B tokens).

Why it’s worth doing. It’s cheap, and the answer matters for #3 and #5: if the gap grows with training, those should be tested at longer budgets too. It’s also the weakest of the five, because the range is still short: the 500M exit only gets to ~120 tokens per parameter, about 50× less than SmolLM2.

2. Every doll as a draft, at a fixed batch size

Why this part: the paper’s speedup is measured on one draft–verifier pair, at batch sizes that differ between the two suites.

Question. In speculative decoding, a small draft model guesses a few tokens ahead and the big verifier checks them all in one pass, keeping the ones it agrees with. The output is the same, just faster. The paper drafts with the 500M, verifies with the 3B, and runs each suite at the largest batch that fits in GPU memory: 102 for Matryoshka, 64 for vanilla. So its +26% (greedy) and +14% (nucleus sampling) speedups mix three effects:

  • more drafted tokens kept per check (+5%, reported for nucleus sampling only);
  • cheaper checking: the verifier reuses the draft’s 24 layers (the whole 500M) instead of recomputing them, roughly 15–20% less compute than a vanilla 3B;
  • a bigger batch, because draft and verifier share one KV cache (the stored attention state of earlier tokens), which leaves memory for more requests.

A nested suite also has more than one possible draft. Each exit’s KV cache is already part of the next one’s, and nesting raises next-token agreement most for the 1.5B–3B pair (+5.7% over the vanilla pair; agreement is what drives acceptance). Yet only 500M → 3B is tested. Does a chain like 500M → 1.5B → 3B do better?

Experiment. Write a decoding loop that keeps one KV cache per block (the released code has no generation). Then test:

  • Chains: 500M → 3B, 1.5B → 3B, 500M → 1.5B → 3B, and n-gram → 500M → 1.5B → 3B. An n-gram draft costs almost nothing, so it can propose tokens for the 500M to check.
  • Small vanilla drafts for the vanilla 3B (vanilla 100M, SmolLM2-135M/360M; they share the tokenizer, so they can draft for these models). Drafts are usually 10–100× smaller than the verifier, and the paper itself shows that a 500M draft barely speeds up the vanilla 3B, so the fair baseline is the best vanilla draft, not that one.
  • Batch sizes of 1 (a single user, where latency is what matters), 64 for both suites (which removes the memory difference), and the maximum (the paper’s setting).

Why it’s worth doing. Multi-level speculation has been tried before, even with a shared KV cache: HiSpec gets 1.28× over a single draft level (Kumar et al., 2026). But its middle levels are early exits, intermediate layers of one network that all have the same width. Here each level is a complete model of its own width, and adding a level costs only its output layer (~0.23 GB). The 3B’s last five layers are about half its compute, and in a chain they only run on tokens the 1.5B already accepted. If the chain wins, nested suites get multi-level speculation almost for free. Separately, the fixed-batch runs split the paper’s speedup into its three parts. None of the released models use grouped-query attention, a standard trick that makes the KV cache several times smaller (Llama-3.2-3B, whose shape the vanilla 3B copies, uses it). With it, sharing the cache saves less memory, so the batch-size gain is probably larger here than it would be in practice.

3. Compare against train-big-then-prune

Why this part: the 36% is measured against the most expensive way to build a suite, not the one people use.

Question. The baseline trains every size from scratch without distillation, even though the paper itself says suite members are “often distilled from larger ones”. The usual recipe today is to train the largest model, prune it (cut layers or width), and then distill: train the smaller model to imitate the big one. Minitron derives 8B and 4B models from a 15B this way, “with up to 40x fewer training tokens per model” (Muralidharan et al., 2024), and Llama 3.2 1B and 3B were pruned from Llama 3.1 8B and trained to match the next-token probabilities (logits) of the 8B and 70B. The paper calls this approach “complementary” because it starts from “a sunk pretraining cost”, but in a suite the largest model gets trained anyway.

The budget. Count training compute as \(6ND\) (6 × parameters × tokens, the usual estimate). A nested suite then costs more than its largest model alone, because each exit has its own output layer, and with a 49K-token vocabulary those layers are big: about 27% more at 200M scale and 5% more at 3B. That extra is what prune-and-distill can spend before it costs more than nesting: about 4–6B distillation tokens per small model at 200M scale (20–30% of pretraining), but only 1–2B at 3B (2–6%). Minitron used under 3% of the original pretraining tokens, so at 3B it’s tight but possible. So it comes down to which approach gives better models.

Experiment. Prune the released vanilla 3B to the 1.5B and 500M shapes, distill each on 1–2B tokens, and compare with the paper’s Table 2. Try it at 200M scale first, where it’s cheap. Count compute both as \(6ND\) and as GPU time, because the two disagree: by \(6ND\) the 3B saving is 35%, but the paper’s 200M-scale “41%” comes out at about 27%. The paper turns GPU-hours into FLOPs using the GPU’s peak speed (Appendix B), and small models trained separately probably use the GPU less efficiently, so the 41% is a real GPU-time saving but overstates the compute saving.

Why it’s worth doing. It tells us whether nesting is the cheapest way to build a suite, or only cheaper than training every size separately, and I don’t know which way it goes. Cutting a 3B down to 500M removes 84% of its parameters, and at that point a pruned model may have lost most of what it inherited. On the other hand, distillation beats ordinary training (up to a compute level that grows with the student’s size) “in settings involving many students or an existing teacher” (Busbridge et al., 2025), and a suite has both: the big model is trained anyway, and there are two smaller ones to teach. If prune-and-distill wins, the main thing nesting still has is a draft that shares the verifier’s weights and cache, which pruning can’t give you.

4. Train the draft for acceptance, not likelihood

Why this part: in a nested suite the draft’s loss is a free choice, and the paper picked it for perplexity, not speed.

Question. A drafted token is accepted with probability \(\beta = \sum_v \min(p_v, q_v)\), the overlap between the draft’s next-token distribution \(q\) and the verifier’s \(p\) (Leviathan et al., 2023). For a given draft size and draft length, that overlap is all that matters for speed. The paper trains its draft for something else: 70% ordinary next-token loss and 30% imitating the 3B (the distillation weight, \(\alpha_d = 0.3\)), with the weight chosen for perplexity. A small draft can’t copy the big model exactly, so it has to compromise, and the best compromise for imitation isn’t the best one for acceptance: “minimizing KL does not guarantee maximizing acceptance rate” (Samarin et al., 2026). How much faster would a draft trained for acceptance be?

Experiment.

  • No training: the authors released small-scale runs (a 50M / 100M / 200M suite) whose names suggest \(\alpha_d\) = 0, 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7. Measure the acceptance between the 50M and 200M exits at the paper’s sampling settings. The paper only reports imitation (KL) and perplexity for these, not acceptance.
  • At 3B: include the undocumented vanilla 500M_35B_distill branch. If it really is a vanilla 500M distilled from the vanilla 3B, comparing it with Matryoshka’s 500M shows how much of the agreement comes from distillation and how much from sharing layers.
  • Then train: replace the imitation loss with reverse KL, Jensen–Shannon or an acceptance loss, and also try training on text the draft generates itself, since that’s what it sees while decoding. Run each as a short cooldown branch from one checkpoint, as the paper does in Appendix G, which is much cheaper than full runs. Train the best loss two ways: into the draft’s output layer only, and into its whole block.

Why it’s worth doing. Work on acceptance-trained drafts usually keeps the verifier frozen; one unrefereed preprint tunes an 8B verifier together with its draft head (a small module on top of the verifier that does the drafting). Here the draft is the verifier’s first block, trained from scratch, so a loss that makes the draft agree more can also change the verifier. That’s why the two training variants matter, and why the verifier’s perplexity should be reported next to every speedup. Don’t expect a big win: LK losses, which train the draft on acceptance directly (Samarin et al., 2026), report up to 8–10% longer accepted length, and the paper’s whole accepted-length gain over vanilla is 5%. A flat result would still be useful, because it would mean agreement is limited by the 1:6 size gap rather than by the loss.

5. Does the big doll need to teach the small ones?

Why this part: the paper always trains all blocks together and never tests what happens if it doesn’t.

Question. When everything trains together, the 1.5B and 3B losses also send gradients into the 500M block, so the small model’s weights are partly shaped by what the bigger models need. Does that help the small exits, and does sharing cost the big one? There are hints that the biggest exit pays a price: in the paper’s 200M-scale ablation (Table 3), the 200M exit is worse than vanilla (15.62 vs 15.21 perplexity), while the 100M exit beats its vanilla model.

Experiment. Four runs at 200M scale, with the same tokens and the paper’s per-exit loss weights (the paper blames part of the gap on those weights, Appendix G):

  • (A) Joint: the paper’s recipe (already released).
  • (B) Stop-gradient at every junction (where one block’s output feeds the next): each block learns only from its own exit, but all blocks still train at the same time.
  • (C) Sequential growth: train the 50M on its own (the released vanilla 50M has exactly this shape, so this step is already done), freeze it, add and train the 100M block, freeze that, then add the 200M.
  • (D) (C) plus a short joint fine-tune at the end.

Why it’s worth doing. If (B) matches (A), the gradients coming down from the bigger models aren’t needed. If (C) matches too, a suite can grow after release: you train only a new, bigger block on top of the frozen ones, and the existing models don’t change. I couldn’t find anyone who has done this. Greedy local learning trains each block on its own local loss with no gradients between blocks, which is close to (B), but its per-block heads are thrown away after training, so the blocks never become usable models (Moon et al., 2026). LLaMA Pro grows a model by training new blocks around frozen ones, but the old model doesn’t survive as a working exit of the new one (Wu et al., 2024). If they fall short, joint training is what makes nesting work.
entry.summary: Five follow-ups that test the paper's efficiency claims, all starting from checkpoints the authors have already released.

entry.title: Follow-ups of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

link.title: Follow-ups of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

entry.content:
The paper (Godey & Artzi, 2026) mostly aims at efficiency gains, but I believe there is real interpretability work to be had from its setup. Some of these follow-ups require post-training, but others can be run as-is on the released checkpoints:

1. What does the upper block add?

Question: On which kinds of tokens and contexts does a bigger sub-model outperform a smaller one? I think this is different from comparing models of different sizes, since these share a joint backbone up to some point. Can we measure where the added block helps: on rare tokens, factual recall, arithmetic, etc.?

Experiment: Some metrics would require a different training dataset and some question-answering post-training, but we can already run two interesting experiments:

  • Run the full suite on factual claims from the training data, framed as a sentence-completion task.
  • Evaluate each sub-model, and a vanilla (independently trained) model of the same size, on the same claims.

Why? If additional capabilities are discernible, they must come from parameters outside the first block, which may tell us something about the minimal depth or width a capability needs. Additionally, these are inference-time experiments only, so they require no retraining and can use the published checkpoints.

2. Embedding analysis

Question: The junction, as shown in the visualization post, feeds sub-model \(m+1\) with the (rescaled) output of sub-model \(m\), \(\tilde{o}^m\), concatenated with \(D_{m+1}-D_m\) dimensions of a fresh embedding, \(e^{m+1}\). Analyzing how the block uses these two distinct groups of channels, or analyzing the embeddings themselves, might teach us something about how the work is “divided” between the blocks, or where their additional capabilities emerge from.

Experiment:

  • Analyze the attention heads in the first layer of any block other than the first. Attention selects positions, not channels, so the question is which channels a head reads from: are there heads whose query, key and value weights read mostly from the \(o\) channels? Mostly from the \(e\) channels? This can be measured from the weights alone, before running anything.
    • If such heads are found, try to find their “purpose”: what do they do?
  • Do the two groups get mixed? After the first layer of a block the residual stream mixes the channels, so the clean split only exists at its input. Each sub-model keeps its own LM head, so on deeper layers of the larger block we can apply sub-model \(m\)’s head to the first \(D_m\) channels and read off its predictions directly. This is a logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) that needs no training, unlike the tuned lens (Belrose et al., 2023), and it uses a head that was trained on exactly these channels, which the usual logit lens on intermediate layers is not. Do these predictions change, and by how much (cross-entropy on the logits as well as argmax agreement)?
  • Instead of feeding block 2 with \([o^1, e^2]\), try feeding it \([e^1, e^2]\) and see what happens. This ablation is missing from the paper (its “zero junction” ablation zeroes the fresh embedding but keeps \(o\)). Retrained this way, the larger model becomes a shallower model, which will surely be worse. But the size of the gap is the point: it separates how much the first sub-model’s computation helps the second from how much comes from the added layers and width alone.

Why? Models have emergent capabilities, and pointing out the specific components that give rise to a trait is a big part of interpretability. This architecture reduces the search space and might help locate such answers.

3. Will post-training trickle down?

Question: If post-training is applied to the full suite, what happens to the sub-models? The paper itself lists instruction tuning and alignment of nested suites as an open question, and the critique by achi-or argues it is critical for the paper’s real-world claims to hold.

Experiment: Post-train the whole suite on a simple target (SFT, question answering, refusal training), then ask:

  • Do the smaller sub-models also show the same behaviors?
  • Did the smaller sub-models drift away from being usable stand-alone models?
    • This will probably need some ablations and sweeps to find the limits.
  • How does each sub-model perform on specific tasks, such as question answering or refusal tests?

Why? Post-training is a crucial and expensive part of LLM training in the real world. It would also be interesting to see how such training regimes affect this architecture, given the glimpse it offers into the model’s “inner thoughts” before it answers. This is especially interesting for refusal, which in conventionally trained models is mediated by a single direction in the residual stream (Arditi et al., 2024) and appears to depend on a specific range of middle layers (Li et al., 2025).

What each one costs

  • #1 is the cheapest: inference only, on the released checkpoints. A comparison to vanilla models of the same size would require training those baselines.
  • #2 is mostly inference too: the head analysis needs only the weights, and the lens needs only forward passes. The \([e^1, e^2]\) ablation is the exception, since it means retraining a suite.
  • #3 is the most expensive: post-training a whole suite, plus the sweeps needed to find where the sub-models stop being usable on their own.
entry.summary: The nested suite was built for efficiency, but its shared backbone makes it a ready-made interpretability testbed.

entry.title: A new way of speculative decoding and on policy distillation

link.title: A new way of speculative decoding and on policy distillation

entry.content:
The Teacher Is a Direction, Not a Destination: Extrapolating RL-Induced Representation Residuals in On-Policy Distillation (Hao Li, MeiJia Chen, Weijie Ren, Donghan Li, Zijun Tian, Jingchun Huang, Naibo Wang) this paper introduce a new method to on policy distillation called RIDE, that try to make the student model surpass the teacher rather to simply imitate it.

WaveFront Decoding: Parallelized Self-Speculative Decoding for Looped Language Models (Hyeongju Ha, Jae-Joon Kim) this paper introduce a new way for speculative decoding for looped language models, that parallelizes token drafting and verification across different recurrence depths, significantly accelerating inference without requiring an additional draft model.
entry.summary: 2 papers that expand on ideas used in the matryoshka suits paper.

entry.title: Literature review of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

link.title: Literature review of Matryoshka Language Model Suites

entry.content:
The papers this builds on

Godey and Artzi (2026) (hereafter GA26) introduce Matryoshka LM Suites, which combines nested models, knowledge distillation, and speculative decoding. Its new contribution is how these ideas are integrated to train a family of models.

The nesting principle draws on earlier work. Kusupati et al. (2022) trained embeddings whose initial coordinates already form useful representations, allowing shorter vectors to be used when resources are limited. Building on this idea, Devvrit et al. (2024) applied the nesting principle to Transformer feed-forward networks in MatFormer. Smaller versions use subsets of neurons and share their weights with larger versions. These choices can then be combined across layers to obtain additional sizes without retraining.

Within this line of work, GA26 changes how the models are nested. Larger models extend smaller ones with additional, wider Transformer layers. Its 500M model has 24 layers of width 1024; the 1.5B model adds 10 layers of width 2304; and the 3B model adds another five of width 4352. Smaller models therefore use fewer, narrower layers and smaller attention caches. In the original MatFormer formulation, attention dimensions and depth remain fixed, so reducing the feed-forward width does not shrink the KV cache.

MatFormer has also been adopted at larger scales. Gemma 3n (2025) used MatFormer, nesting a model with 2B effective parameters inside one with 4B (Gemma Team, 2025). GA26’s trained comparison with MatFormer is limited to the 200M scale, while Appendix E compares theoretical resource costs at a 3B size. A direct comparison of model quality at larger scales remains an interesting question.

To train the nested models, GA26 also draws on knowledge distillation. Buciluǎ et al. (2006) demonstrated that small models could learn to imitate larger ensembles. Building on this approach, Hinton et al. (2015) described combining supervision from correct labels with the teacher’s predicted probabilities. GA26 uses this loss form for next-token prediction. Its contribution here is the integration, where one shared training forward pass supplies the predictions needed for the largest model to teach all smaller models.

This agreement between models also benefits speculative decoding, which lets a small model propose several tokens that a larger model checks. This can accelerate generation while preserving the larger model’s output distribution (Leviathan et al., 2023). Earlier work improved this process by training the small model to imitate the large one, i.e., by draft–verifier alignment through distillation Zhou et al. (2024). GA26 combines these benefits within its model suite, since distillation encourages agreement during training, while shared layers reduce duplicated work during inference.

The fields and concepts it connects to

The use of smaller models within a larger network also connects conceptually to the lottery ticket hypothesis Frankle and Carbin (2019). They showed that a large trained network contains much smaller sub-networks that, trained alone from the same starting weights, reach similar accuracy. Finding them, however,requires training the large network first and then pruning it. The resulting sub-networks are scattered sets of weights. MatFormer and GA26 design the smaller networks in advance. The whole family is then trained together from scratch, and each size can be extracted as a complete model.

Another related approach is elastic compression, which turns an already trained LLM into several smaller versions through additional training (Cai et al., 2024). GA26 instead trains the different networks together from scratch, aiming to reduce the cost of creating new versions.

Finally, LoRA (Hu et al., 2022) adapts a pretrained model by freezing its original weights and learning small, low-rank updates. Its connection to GA26 is the broader goal of reducing training costs through parameter reuse. However, LoRA’s updates still require the base model’s weights, whereas GA26 jointly trains complete models of different sizes with shared weights. LoRA is therefore a related efficiency technique.
entry.summary: Ideas behind Matryoshka LM Suites and what it adds
